newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: APEC faces terrorist threat, ducks trade challenge.
newsitem.headline: APEC faces terrorist threat, ducks trade challenge.

text.p: APEC faced up to a terrorist threat but ducked a challenge on free trade ahead of its fourth summit in the Philippines, seen as a test of its credibility as it seeks to forge a free trade zone embracing half of humanity.
Finance and trade ministers of 18 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) members failed to endorse a U.S. initiative for free trade in information technology by 2000.
Instead, they appeared to bow to objections from Asian sceptics, including Malaysia, by agreeing on a vaguely worded statement of support to put before the Subic Bay summit on Monday.

The diplomatic fudge exposed the divisions between the developed nations of APEC -- including the United States and Japan -- and developing countries who believe APEC should advance on the basis of consensus, not rules and timetables.
It did nothing to silence critics who say APEC's goal of a free trade and investment zone circling the Pacific by 2020 is an unworkable dream.
A U.S. official early on Friday warned American diplomats, journalists and others they might be targets of terrorist attack in the Philippines.

Security sources said police were worried leftist groups may be planning bombings and assassinations to disrupt the summit, to be attended by U.S. President Bill Clinton, Chinese President Jiang Zemin and other key leaders.
An intelligence report obtained by Reuters indicated explosives found at Manila's airport on Wednesday were not part of a security drill, as reported at the time, but a real bomb.
Two leftist activists were arrested on Wednesday night, one on charges of illegal possession of ammunition and the other of possessing subversive literature.

Philippine President Fidel Ramos, whose zeal for free trade has transformed his nation from "sick man of Asia" to Asian tiger, urged 450 top businessmen from APEC nations to "go, go, go" for a borderless economy circling the Pacific.

Indeed, the business world, unlike the politicians, appears to be moving forward quickly. More than $2 billion worth of new deals and numerous business relationships are being forged in Manila in what has been billed as the largest networking event of the year, businessmen from APEC member economies said on Friday.

"We hope that in the next few days all of us will benefit...," said Roberto Romulo, chairman of the APEC Business Advisory Council at the start of the three-day APEC Business Forum which Ramos addressed.

At the APEC conference itself, a Manila Action Plan, which stitches together market-opening initiatives of all APEC members, made clear the grouping lacks the ability to ensure trade barriers will actually fall.
The plans are so comprehensive they are "without parallel in other trade and investment liberalisation fora", according to an advance copy obtained by Reuters.

But only five of the 18-member economies have spelled out how they are going to reach APEC's stated goal of lowering all tariff barriers by 2010 for developed members like the United States and Japan and by 2020 for the less well-off.
The five are Brunei, Chile, Hong Kong, New Zealand and Singapore.
The action plan also admits that the loose grouping lacks the teeth to enforce these commitments.
Clinton, Jiang and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and other APEC leaders are expected to endorse the plan at their summit.

The plan to open up trade in information equipment was widely viewed as a test of APEC's resolve to stamp its mark on the World Trade Organisation, which holds its first ministerial meeting next month in Singapore.
U.S. officials said the fight to liberalise trade in computers, memory chips and telecommunications equipment worth an annual $1.8 trillion would continue.
Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said that information technology products would be to the 21st century "what roads and bridges were to the 19th century".
"We must keep pace with infrastructure requirements of the 21st century and we must in that sense put our money where our mouth is," she said.
The ministers agreed to refine criteria for new APEC members.
"New members will be announced in Kuala Lumpur in 1998 and will be admitted and participate in New Zealand in 1999," said Philippine foreign ministry undersecretary Rodolfo Severino.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), six of whose members are in APEC, has been pushing for quick membership for the other ASEAN member, Vietnam.

Severino said 11 nations -- including Vietnam, India, Pakistan, Russia, Colombia, Peru, Ecuador and Mongolia -- had expressed interest in joining. But some members, including the United States, were opposed to rapid expansion.
